verifier.reason: The facts reproduce. operating-calendar.yml failed on all 32 runs from 2026-09-30 to 2026-10-31, after a last success on 09-29. scripts/operating_calendar.py lists 6 OVERDUE rituals (fullreview-delta, rhythm-checkpoint-30d, fullreview-full, accuracy-full, managed-where-reverify, emf-series-census) and 17 expired carry-forward lens grades at 56 days. No open issue tracks the calendar; #2800, #2832 and #3919 are all closed. The premise of 'no owner visibility' is weaker than stated, though. HANDOVER_LATEST.md:47 names the expired lenses and the OVERDUE fullreview-full/accuracy-full as the next action, with a run order, and boot_brief.py reads operating_calendar.py at SessionStart. Three of the six overdue rituals (fullreview-full, fullreview-delta, accuracy-full) are cleared by the /review run now in progress. The residual defect is narrower: managed-where-reverify (hard date 09-30), emf-series-census (hard date 10-08) and rhythm-checkpoint-30d are overdue with no owning issue or handover line. Separately, no tenure rule turns a workflow red that persists for N days into a tracked item, as ALARM_TENURE does for alarms. Whether that warrants new auto-file machinery is an ADR-103 rent question the finding does not price.
verifier.reproduction: `gh run list --workflow operating-calendar.yml --limit 40` shows 32 consecutive daily failures from 2026-09-30 to 10-31, preceded by successes from 09-22 to 09-29. `python3 scripts/operating_calendar.py` ends with '❌ 6 ritual(s) OVERDUE: fullreview-delta, rhythm-checkpoint-30d, fullreview-full, accuracy-full, managed-where-reverify, emf-series-census' and 17 'stale carry-forward' lines. `gh issue list --state all --search 'operating-calendar in:title,body'` finds no open calendar issue. `grep -n -i operating.calendar handovers/HANDOVER_LATEST.md` matches line 47 (fullreview-full/accuracy-full named as OVERDUE).
verifier.root_cause_check: Part of the cause is wrong. The red is the calendar working as designed: it screams until each ritual's artifact lands, and the owner is told through the handover and boot brief. The true gap is narrower: three non-review rituals have no owner, and nothing tracks how long a workflow has been red, so a long red becomes background noise.

verifier.reason: Narrowly confirmed at P3, but the finder's framing needs two corrections. (1) The stale path is real: lambdas/numeric.py does not exist (ls: No such file), and the HAE comment at lambdas/ingestion/health_auto_export_lambda.py:214 still points to it. (2) The 'DELIBERATELY divergent' claim is now false, not just stale. Canonical lambdas/common/numeric.py:47 already maps NaN and Inf to None (lines 53-56) and takes precision=, so the HAE copy (lines 212-225) behaves the same as floats_to_decimal(obj, precision=4) and is redundant. (3) A name-regex guard already exists: tests/test_ddb_patterns.py::test_d5_no_forked_floats_to_decimal (lines 350-387). It has an allow-list with reasons that names character_sheet_lambda._dec. Its gap: it describes health_auto_export as a 'try/except ImportError fallback shim', but the HAE def is unconditional with no import attempt, and its regex cannot match the public name floats_to_decimal or _dec. Of the six _dec helpers the finder lists, four are scalar coercers (time_affluence:347, illness_triad:287, coach_calibration:283, coach_baseline:200). d5 records scalar coercers as a 'genuinely different contract', so those four are not defects. lambdas/health/milestone_ledger.py:406 is a recursive walker with no NaN guard (line 414-415: float -> Decimal(str(obj))) that is not in d5's documented list; that is the one real unlisted fork. Related closed issues: #1207, #3538.
verifier.reproduction: ls lambdas/numeric.py -> No such file; sed -n 210,225p lambdas/ingestion/health_auto_export_lambda.py (comment cites lambdas/numeric.py; body = isnan/isinf->None, round 4); sed -n 47,75p lambdas/common/numeric.py (NaN/Inf->None + precision=); sed -n 337,353p tests/test_ddb_patterns.py (_FORBIDDEN_DECIMAL_DEF matches only _to_decimal|_decimalize*|_float_to_decimal|_floats_to_decimal|to_decimal; HAE described as an ImportError shim); grep 'def floats_to_decimal' lambdas/ mcp/ -> 2 defs (common/numeric.py:47, health_auto_export_lambda.py:212); sed -n 406,416p lambdas/health/milestone_ledger.py (recursive, no NaN branch).
verifier.root_cause_check: Corrected cause: the #1207 consolidation guard (d5) matches by fork name, and its allow-list misdescribes the HAE copy as an ImportError shim. So an unconditional public-name copy and a recursive `_dec` walker (milestone_ledger) slip past it. Fix within the existing guard: delete the HAE copy in favour of floats_to_decimal(precision=4), and widen d5 to recursive walkers (AST: a self-recursive def with a float->Decimal branch), keeping the scalar allow-list. A new invariant test is not needed.

findings_refuted.regression_guard: A CDK/live-config drift test pinning the MCP AllowOrigins to the known claude.ai and desktop callback origins, or a one-line ADR note recording * as chosen because the bearer carries auth.

verifier.reason: The live config reproduces: AllowOrigins ["*"], AuthType NONE, and an unauthenticated POST returns 401. The claimed harm does not hold. CORS controls whether a browser page may read the response to a request that carries ambient credentials (cookies). This endpoint authenticates with a bearer header, which the caller must supply explicitly. Anyone holding a stolen bearer can use it from curl or any server whatever the CORS setting, so pinning origins would not reduce that risk at all. Remote MCP connectors call from the server side, so they never depend on browser origin checks either. The URL is deliberately not CDK-managed, and possession of the URL plus HMAC bearer auth is the documented boundary (cdk/stacks/mcp_stack.py:8-10, 114-121, SEC-02 #780). A drift test pinning origins would add standing machinery with no security benefit, which fails the ADR-103 cost test. At most, the ADR note the finding suggests is a one-line documentation nicety, not a P3 defect.
verifier.reproduction: `aws lambda get-function-url-config --function-name life-platform-mcp --region us-west-2` returns Cors.AllowOrigins ["*"], AllowHeaders includes authorization and x-api-key, AuthType NONE. `curl -X POST <url> -d '{}'` returns 401. `grep -n 'Function URL' cdk/stacks/mcp_stack.py` gives line 114: 'deliberately NOT CDK-managed'.
verifier.root_cause_check: With bearer auth and no cookies, CORS is not a security control, so a wildcard origin exposes nothing.

verifier.reason: The ledger numbers reproduce, but both parts of the premise are wrong. (1) The alarm had not cleared when it was renewed. The agent only collects alarms in ALARM state (remediation/agent.py:625, describe_alarms(StateValue='ALARM')). qa-smoke-failures was in ALARM from 2026-10-27T04:53Z to 2026-10-30T18:31Z, and the renewal at 17:45Z on 10-30 falls inside that span. 'Self-cleared' in the conclusion refers to that day's metric value, which ran ahead of the 1-day-period alarm state. (2) A retirement condition and a cap both already exist. Entries are dropped at the 7-day ACK_TTL_DAYS expiry if not re-acked (update_ack_ledger). The #1960 ratchet (ACK_MAX_RENEWALS=3) stops annotating an exhausted ack, and ack_ratchet_escalations re-escalates it to needs_human every run while it is still in ALARM. A renewals=114 entry is not working as an ack, so the counter is cosmetic. The real pattern underneath is that qa-smoke-failures flaps (5 transitions since 10-20). That is a different finding.

findings_confirmed.summary: An owner-approved ceiling raise took effect in code about 5 days after approval, and the governor kept enforcing the old $215 ceiling in between. Reader narratives were probably paused under tier 2 in that gap.
findings_confirmed.evidence: The $300 window was approved 2026-10-18 (ceiling_window.reason on /api/receipts). Its commit b42051824 (#5148) is dated 2026-10-23 12:02 -0700. The window is a hard-coded constant, _TEMP_CEILING_WINDOW = (date(2026,10,1), date(2026,11,1)) at cost_governor_lambda.py:263. SSM budget-tier history: 10-19T17:00 -> 2, 10-23T17:00 -> 0. MTD history: 10-19 $157.20, which is 52% of $300 but 73% of $215. Under $215, actual tier 1 plus the +1 cap allows tier 2; under $300 it would not. That the old ceiling caused the tier 2 is inference from these numbers, not a log read. I found no governor log group to confirm it. Tier 2 pauses reader narratives (/api/receipts tier_semantics, budget_guard ladder).

verifier.reason: The gap is real. The owner approved the raise on 2026-10-18 (ADR-133 amendment at docs/DECISIONS.md:4525, quoting his words). PR #5148 was opened 2026-10-19T02:13Z and merged 2026-10-23T19:02Z (commit b42051824, Fri Oct 23 12:02 -0700). In between, SSM /life-platform/budget-tier went to 2 at 2026-10-19T17:00-07:00 and fell back to 0 at 2026-10-23T17:00-07:00, the first governor run after the merge. The tier flipped on the day forecast and cleared on the first run after the merge. So the claim that the old ceiling caused tier 2 is backed by the platform's own forecast, not only by the finder's arithmetic. No log line confirms it. No existing issue or INCIDENT_LOG row records the 4-day lag: the gh search for ceiling window or owner pin returned nothing relevant, and #5135 is about the dev-session envelope.
